texts: bad: the substance is gone — no atom mentions mire-essence, so the KB records only that a typical day yields several vessels, because a container-of-a-mass "of"-phrase (the "a cup of water" case) has no encoding. Give the contents their own finite clause: "A typical day yields several vessels, and those vessels hold mire-essence."
good. the day is a witness, the four vessels become a group carrying an exact count, and "heavy-thread day" decomposes to its head genus as required.

bad: the numeral is dropped — the parse says only that the day yields a vessel, so "one vessel" and "a vessel" become the same claim, since a count atom has a slot only on a plural group (as in your "four vessels" sentence). Rewrite so the singleness is a word the translator can keep: "A thin day yields a single vessel." The exactly-one content then survives as a stated property of the vessel rather than vanishing.

mixed: the "in deep winter" window rides the reified thin-state, but the parse also emits a flat "the thread harvest is thin" with no season attached, so the KB reads as thin all year round. A bare-plural kind subject routes the whole claim into a season-conditioned property and emits no unrestricted half: "Thread harvests are thin in deep winter."

bad: the conditional came out inverted — the draining landed in the rule's conclusion, so instead of "thin harvest once a wraith drains", the parse asserts that every wraith drains the lanterns and thins the harvest. Write the trigger as an explicit whenever-clause so it is matched rather than asserted: "Whenever a wraith drains the lanterns, the thread harvest turns thin."

mixed: the conditional itself is right (empty basket → each cauldron idle), but "sit" has no carrier as a postural verb with an adjective complement and is dropped, so only "idle" survives. Use the plain copula, which costs nothing here: "When the thread basket is empty, the cauldrons are idle." Be aware that either way the rule, once fired, leaves the cauldrons idle permanently — there is no way yet to tie the state to the occasion.

bad: beside the windowed state the parse emits the unrestricted kind claim "distillation is heavy", so the KB says distillation is heavy all year and the "from early autumn to Lantern-night" window survives only as a side atom. A from/to window has no slot on a bare "is", but it lands cleanly on an event's start and end — the frame your "Distillation recovers from the spring equinox to the summer solstice" already uses: "Distillation runs heavily from early autumn to Lantern-night."

bad: the bare kind word "distillation" sits in the role slot of a single flat event, so the parse reads as one thinning of the kind itself rather than the seasonal regularity you mean — a mass/process noun as the subject of a habitual clause has no defined route. Give the clause a concrete bearer: "The distillation yield thins through deep winter."
good. "from … to …" lands on the start and end of the recover event, the named times stay bare constants, and the present tense correctly adds no tense atom.

good. judged acceptable on adjudication — the manner adverb keeps its surface form and the habitual reading is right; only the spanning force of "through" goes unrecorded, and that is a known gap in the instruction set rather than a fault in your wording.
